title: The covenant prayer
hook: Methodists renew their covenant each year: I am no longer my own, but yours

segments.voice: Yesterday, the class meeting: how is it with your soul? Your line was watch over one another. Who did you ask, and what did you hear back? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

Joshua, old now, gathers the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He reminds them of everything God has done, and then he puts it to them plainly: choose whom you will serve. And he answers first, for himself: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." The people answer too, and that day, the book says, Joshua made a covenant with them. A promise already made, made again. Methodists do something like that once a year, at a covenant service. The congregation renews its promise to God, in words that aren't easy to say. Today's word is the prayer at its heart: the covenant prayer.

Covenant is a word the Bible keeps coming back to. In Hebrew it's berit, and it runs from Noah to Abraham to Sinai. Jeremiah looks ahead to a new one, where God says, "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." Not carved on stone this time. Written inside. John Wesley took up a practice from Puritan writers before him, a yearly renewal of that covenant, and gave it to the Methodists. The prayer Methodists say today is short, and it's hard. It begins with today's line: I am no longer my own, but yours. Then it hands everything over, the pleasant and the painful together. Put me to doing, or to suffering. Use me, or set me aside. Let me be full, or empty. Let me have all things, or nothing. It isn't asking for suffering. It's refusing to make faithfulness depend on comfort. That's the surprise in it. Plenty of promises come with conditions; this one tries to have none. Paul gives the ground for it: "ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price." Christian teaching reads that price as Christ's own life. And the prayer doesn't end in loss. It turns around at the close, and the one who gave everything away hears that God is theirs too. It sounds like the Song of Songs: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Why say it every year? Because people drift. A covenant, like a marriage, gets spoken again so it doesn't get forgotten.

Here's the practice: stand at the edge of that prayer. Let your breath settle. Notice what you'd find hardest to hand over: a plan, a comfort, a person, being needed. Don't argue with it. Just see it. If you pray, you can say the prayer's first line slowly, I am no longer my own, but yours, and stop there, letting it sink in. If you don't, simply name the thing once, quietly, and let it sit there without grabbing it back. The bell holds the time.
The covenant prayer. The Methodist prayer of yielding everything to God, said each year when the covenant is renewed.
Your line: no longer my own. Today, give one hour away without counting it: to a person, a task or a need that isn't yours. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Methodists hold a covenant service once a year, often around the new year, where the congregation renews its covenant with God and prays the covenant prayer together.

pairs: as for me and my house

myth: the covenant prayer asks God only for good things
it offers both: doing and suffering, being used and set aside, full and empty.

"as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

fork.setup: you're at a covenant service. the prayer offers God your plenty and your emptiness alike. what does it hold back?
fork.reveal: nothing. it hands over the pleasant and the painful together, and then turns around: the one who gave everything hears that God is theirs too.

original.note: Hebrew: covenant — the word in Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a contract with God: I'll do this if you do that.
what it means: a promise offered without conditions, renewed each year, answered by God's own promise.
what a scholar hears: berit runs from Noah through Sinai to Jeremiah 31's new covenant written on the heart; Wesley's service took up a Puritan practice of renewing it.
recall: a psalm in rhyme and steady meter

notes: Editor pass: 'one of the Bible's great words' softened; 'Christians hear' reworded as Christian teaching; practice no longer uses open hands on the lap (repeated days 1163 and 1170).

The covenant prayer is described and paraphrased, not quoted: the widely used 'traditional' wording appears in twentieth-century Methodist service books and its copyright status is unclear. Only the index line 'I am no longer my own, but yours' is spoken (index form uses 'yours'). Confirm.
Wesley's debt to Puritan covenant renewals (Joseph and Richard Alleine) is stated without names or dates; confirm.
howItsDone says 'often around the new year'; confirm this is fair for Methodist practice.
'Most promises come with conditions' is a general observation about promises, not a claim about a tradition.
Covenant arc (Noah, Abraham, Sinai, Jeremiah) is general; Jeremiah 31:31 uses 'new covenant' (בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה). Confirm original note.
Audit pass: the short covenant prayer used today is a later Methodist abridgment, not Wesley's own longer text (from Richard Alleine); teach now says 'the prayer Methodists say today'. Confirm.
